item.title: Houston, Do We Have A Problem?
item.dc:creator: ovaughn
item.description: The midterm election results have important implications for the US macro outlook, with a more challenging environment for the AI investment cycle, a potentially accelerated resolution to the Iran conflict and a political realignment towards the centre ahead of 2028 . item.content:encoded:
The midterm election results have important implications for the US macro outlook, with a more challenging environment for the AI investment cycle, a potentially accelerated resolution to the Iran conflict and a political realignment towards the centre ahead of 2028. The electoral backlash against data-centre development introduces new constraints on the pace of AI infrastructure deployment, although the geographical mobility of capital should limit the ultimate impact on aggregate investment. The more immediate consequences are likely to be slower construction, greater execution risk and a redistribution of returns along the AI supply chain, favouring businesses with operational and energized compute over hardware suppliers exposed to deployment delays. For index level risk assets, these headwinds may be offset if the Iran war reaches a quicker diplomatic settlement than previously expected. The scale of the Republican defeat may create some urgency in Washington to negotiate which could align with Tehran’s apparent incentive to monetise its remaining leverage. Meanwhile, the breadth of the swing against Republicans, alongside the relative outperformance of centrist Democrats, suggests a political recalibration towards the centre as both parties look ahead to 2028. We therefore see competing forces for equities, likely to manifest in a “Peak Capex” rotation, but a more consistent directional impulse for rates, with slower near-term investment, a marginal reduction in near term financing demand and the prospect of lower energy prices all favouring lower yields.

The election suggests the data-centre buildout may face a tougher regulatory and permitting environment. 56% of voters described AI and data centres as a crucial or major factor in their congressional vote and voters opposed data centre development in at least 39 of the 45 local ballot initiatives on the issue. The potential exposure is substantial, with around 45 GW across 350 projects in Texas, Ohio, Pennsylvania and Georgia at risk between 2026–30, including 24 GW in Texas alone, a state accounting for a substantial share of planned/marginal US capacity by 2030. Viewed through the lens of general equilibrium, however, the impact on aggregate investment is likely to be considerably smaller, as restrictions in one jurisdiction create incentives for capital and construction to migrate elsewhere eventually. Provided demand for compute remains strong, restrictions in one jurisdiction should encourage investment to migrate towards others willing and able to accommodate it, with the scarcity of available capacity sustaining the incentive to build. Securing alternative sites, power and approvals takes time, so this adjustment could still materially delay deployment and raise costs. We would therefore expect some moderation in the near-term growth and inflation impulse from construction and associated resource demand, alongside a smaller impact on cumulative investment and financing requirements.

The rotational consequences of the election we think diverge sharply along the supply chain, with markets increasingly likely to chase a “peak AI capex” theme, rotating out of memory, neoclouds and energy, and into staples, healthcare, banks, housing, retail and, in line with our Tokenomics 2.0 view: the hyperscalers themselves. The underlying intuition is that a slower buildout could be relatively favourable for those doing the spending, and potentially less so for those receiving it. For the hardware “picks and shovels”, slower delivery of powered buildings raises the risk that component production runs ahead of installation, leaving suppliers exposed to order deferrals and excess inventories even while usable compute remains scarce; this vulnerability is likely most pronounced in memory, optical and other semiconductor components.

For cloud businesses already selling energised compute, or bringing fully permitted capacity with secured power online shortly, delayed competition should instead support utilisation, pricing power and prospective margins, while reducing the risk of an eventual capacity glut. For the hyperscalers themselves, some moderation in the pace of capital expenditure should also provide relief to free cash flow and financing requirements. With CBRE reporting just 1.4% vacancy across its primary North American markets and 80.4% of capacity under construction already preleased, additional barriers to entry should reinforce the scarcity value of operational assets. The relative beneficiaries should therefore be the businesses able to supply compute now, with a stronger claim on the economics of the investment cycle as physical expansion becomes harder. This should also create considerable scope for differentiation through stock selection, with the geographical distribution of development pipelines, particularly exposure to Texas and other jurisdictions facing tighter permitting restrictions, becoming an increasingly important determinant of execution risk, the timing of revenue realisation and ultimately relative valuations.

For risk assets in aggregate, we still see slower deployment and greater execution risk as an adverse development, notwithstanding the rotation towards sectors less exposed to the AI investment cycle. While the election removes an important source of political uncertainty, the argument for treating it as a clearing event seems less compelling when the outcome itself implies a more challenging investment environment for the AI build out, particularly given the extent of the swing was larger than expected. For rates, the combination of risk aversion, a potentially softer near-term investment impulse and possible modest financing deferrals should favour lower yields, although the geographical mobility of capital suggests caution in extrapolating this into a lasting collapse in either spending or issuance.

The scale and breadth of the demographic swing against Republicans suggest that Trump’s governing choices have weakened the coalition that returned him to office. The Iran war, tariffs and renewed pressure on household purchasing power appear to have undermined his affordability agenda, with the sharp rise in gasoline and diesel prices particularly damaging for rural and agricultural communities across the Midwest, where Republican losses have been pronounced. The overlap between higher fuel-price exposure and the swing against Republicans is striking, suggesting that the economic consequences of Trump’s policy choices have been felt particularly acutely in parts of his traditional electoral base.

Relative to the 2022 midterms, the Republican advantage among men has disappeared, having stood at 14 points, while its lead among white men has narrowed from 28 to 12 points. Even among white men without a college degree, arguably the most historically dependable constituency in the Republican electoral base, the margin has fallen from 46 to 30. The Republican advantage among non-college graduates more broadly has declined from 12 to four points, and among voters over 65 from 12 to three, while the Democratic margin among women has widened from eight to 18 points and among college graduates from ten to 26. These appear to be substantial reversals extending deep into the Republican base, consistent with voters responding to economic outcomes that may have fallen short of expectations. Alongside what looks like an erosion of Trump’s 2024 gains among younger and Hispanic voters, the results may leave Republicans weighing both the consequences of his policy choices and the potential fragility of a highly personalised coalition that may not persist without the President on the ballot in 2028.

We think that combination strengthens the case for a more conventional Republican nominee capable of recovering the political centre in 2028. Prediction markets have already begun repricing this shifting balance of power. For example, Ron DeSantis’s implied probability of securing the nomination has risen from roughly 4% before the results to around 19%, while JD Vance’s has fallen from approximately 36% to 31%, leaving him the favourite but with a diminished advantage. We are inclined to read the DeSantis move primarily as an increased premium on distance from the administration’s governing record. The Republican party could find itself carrying the liabilities of Trump’s time in office without the candidate-specific turnout advantages that helped assemble a broad but ultimately less stable coalition of voters.

We see two further important implications of the election for the strategic US macro outlook. First, the Democratic resurgence appears to have been considerably stronger among more centrist candidates than those on the party’s left flank. Across the 17 states that held Senate races in both 2024 and 2026, the average Democratic swing relative to the 2024 presidential election was 6.7 percentage points, but this fell to just 3.1 points among candidates endorsed by Bernie Sanders, compared with 8.1 points for those without his endorsement. While these comparisons may have been influenced by differences in state electorates and candidate characteristics, we think the divergence is striking given the scale of the national swing, suggesting that the electorate’s repudiation of the Trump administration should not necessarily be interpreted as an endorsement of a substantially more progressive economic agenda. The results may therefore strengthen the influence of the Democratic Party’s more moderate wing as attention turns towards 2028, with implications for the eventual direction of fiscal, tax and regulatory policy.

Furthermore, the election may have materially increased the political urgency of bringing the Iran war to a conclusion. Both President Trump and Vice President Vance have attributed Republican losses, at least in part, to the conflict, reinforcing the political costs of prolonging a war whose consequences for energy prices and household purchasing power have been particularly damaging among traditional Republican constituencies. We argued in Iran – Peak Gamma that Tehran’s strategic position resembled a long, high-strike oil call expiring around the US midterms, with its capacity to extract political concessions through disruption to energy markets approaching a maximum ahead of the election, before the time value of that leverage evaporated and escalation dominance was lost. Recent diplomatic developments in the immediate lead up to the midterms could be interpreted as a sign that Tehran may indeed be attempting to monetize its remaining leverage through a negotiated settlement. Notably, the election suggests that Washington’s incentives to reach an agreement may also have strengthened, which could bring the political calculus of both sides into closer alignment.

With substantial crude flows already being sustained through and around the Strait of Hormuz, we suspect a credible diplomatic resolution could precipitate further compression in energy risk premia and our analysis of the oil option market implies the market has begun to substantially reduce the upside premium embedded in the last week. Specifically, the three-month option-implied probability of Brent exceeding $120 has more than halved since 28th October, from 23% to 9%, while the one-month probability has collapsed from 27% to just 7%. Upside skew has also flattened across shorter maturities, suggesting that markets have been progressively removing the premium associated with a renewed escalation in the conflict. The direction and concentration of these distributional price adjustments are consistent with our thesis that the midterms could catalyse a resolution.

item.title: Tokenomics 2.0
item.dc:creator: ovaughn
item.description: Consumption weighted token prices have declined approximately 50% over six months and average token prices have declined 62% at the frontier, reflecting both the growing share of cheaper open-weight models and price cuts by proprietary providers, likely driven by some combination...
item.content:encoded:
Consumption weighted token prices have declined approximately 50% over six months and average token prices have declined 62% at the frontier, reflecting both the growing share of cheaper open-weight models and price cuts by proprietary providers, likely driven by some combination of improved inference efficiency and competitive pressure. Increased competition from open-weight models may exert pressure on margins at the frontier through time, but the expansion of token volume suggests overall inference demand is accelerating.

Open-weight models now account for around 65-70% of smart routing token volume, potentially putting pressure on excess rents at the frontier as cheaper models become “good enough” for a growing range of enterprise tasks, especially given US-developed open-weight models offer greater flexibility around customisation, hosting and data control. Caution is warranted in extrapolating from OpenRouter and Vercel data, since users who self-select into model-routing platforms may be more willing to experiment with and switch between models, exhibiting less inertia than the broader AI customer base; however the direction of travel is nevertheless informative, especially as we expect adoption to become increasingly cost-conscious through time.

The recent stall in total expenditure in Ramp’s monthly spend data provides some further grounds for caution, as it shows essentially no growth in overall enterprise spend in the last two months (Aug and Sept), likely reflecting the interaction of lower token prices with increased volume. The data also implies that 80% of spend on frontier labs is driven by 1% of firms, and that the top 1% spent $9,568 per employee per month in Sept vs the median firm that spent $15.7 per employee per month, illustrating how concentrated spending remains. The recent plateau may prove important as total expenditure determines the revenues available to remunerate the AI investment cycle, and it appears that some combination of lower prices and increased competition from open-source may be causing total spend to flatline. The upcoming October release will be important as more timely token volume data from October imply a further acceleration of inference demand, but the implications for total spend remain unclear given shifts in token prices and composition of spend.

Token volumes have risen approximately 5x over the last 6 months and around 50% over the last four weeks, consistent with a substantial demand response as intelligence becomes cheaper. Where that expansion exceeds improvements in computational efficiency, demand for GPU-hours increases, and GPU rental rates suggest that available compute capacity remains scarce: H100 rentals are up approximately 14% over six months and 7% over the last 30 days, while B200 rentals have risen 27.5% over six months, implying robust demand for compute. Continued strength in older H100s is particularly striking against the depreciation one would ordinarily expect from technological obsolescence, implying sellers of scarce compute are well placed to extract rents.

A firm’s margin on each additional unit of output is the difference between its selling price and marginal cost, so falling output prices and rising input costs squeeze margins unless productivity improves sufficiently to compensate. For the frontier labs, competition from cheaper open-weight models can exert both pressures simultaneously, pushing token prices lower whilst stimulating inference demand that bids up the cost of compute. At unchanged inference efficiency, higher GPU rental rates increase the marginal cost of supplying a token, leaving the frontier receiving less for what it sells whilst paying more to produce it. The question is therefore whether improvements in tokens served per GPU-hour (inference efficiency) can offset both the decline in selling prices and the increase in compute costs in perpetuity. Gross margin can be approximated as follows, assuming compute dominates serving costs and holding workload mix constant:

Using the 27.5% rise in B200 GPU rental rates as an illustrative increase in compute costs, combined with the 50% decline in average token prices requires throughput to increase 2.55-fold, merely to preserve the gross-margin. This is not an unsurmountable issue, as reporting suggests that inference efficiency gains in the last year have been substantial, and compute costs can be locked in via multi year deals. However the marginal economics of inference can still remain a source of pressure, particularly on a forward basis, should open source competition intensify, or should progress on inference efficiency stall. These calculations are illustrative only and intended to highlight the efficiency requirement rather than estimate any individual lab’s margins, since public rental benchmarks differ from contracted compute costs and published token prices differ from realised revenues.

Hence, a clear focus is whether inference efficiency gains can continue to support margins despite intense competition for both market share and compute, particularly as the easier improvements or low-hanging fruit may, through time, become exhausted. New hardware offers greater throughput but also commands higher prices, absorbing some of the incremental benefit. Moreover, as efficiency improves, those same benefits may apply to open-weight models too, such that another round of price cuts may stimulate further inference and renew the pressure on scarce compute, leaving the frontier obliged to deliver further successive gains simply to defend its existing margins. None of this implies that the fundamentals of the business model are broken; however, markets move on gaps between expectations and reality, and we question whether expectations for frontier profitability fully accommodate sustained competition that passes efficiency gains through to customers whilst infrastructure suppliers capture the benefits of scarcity in the form of excess rents.

We consequently see a more nuanced outlook for the AI ecosystem, with strong inference demand favouring suppliers of scarce compute as competition raises questions around excess returns at the frontier. The economics may resemble those of airlines and airports, with frontier labs as the established airlines, providing an essential service to the economy in a highly competitive market and sees open-weight models as the low-cost carriers, expanding the market through cheaper fares whilst constraining what incumbents can charge. The hyperscalers’ infrastructure businesses resemble the airports, with stickier demand and greater scope for higher, more durable margins from supplying scarce compute, and a commercial architecture that is model agnostic in the long run. A reassessment of profitability at the frontier on margin or commoditisation concerns would nevertheless be challenging for the complex as a whole, given how much infrastructure investment rests on future spending commitments. Within that framing, we see the hyperscalers as potentially the most durable beneficiaries of growing inference demand, with diversified cash flows and strong balance sheets allowing them to fund additional capacity and withstand a reassessment of frontier profitability more comfortably than leveraged neoclouds.

item.dc:creator: ovaughn

He highlighted the accelerating impact of AI, the growing intersection of technology and national pow...
item.content:encoded:
Jim Esposito, President of Citadel Securities, opened the Future of Global Markets Conference with remarks on the convergence of technological innovation and geopolitical change. He highlighted the accelerating impact of AI, the growing intersection of technology and national power and the critical role of capital markets in financing the next era of economic transformation.

Key Takeaways

  • Technology and Geopolitics: Rapid technological advancement and geopolitical shifts are reshaping the global order, with computing power, energy and capital increasingly becoming instruments of national power.
  • AI Beyond the Digital World: AI is moving into factories, laboratories, transportation, energy systems and defense, expanding the boundaries of innovation.
  • Capital Fuels Innovation: Like the Industrial Revolution, today’s technological transformation has the potential to create entirely new industries, with capital markets playing a critical role in financing their development.
  • Citadel Securities at Scale: With 1,800+ professionals globally, Citadel Securities executes roughly a quarter of U.S. equity trading volume and processes nearly $800 billion in daily notional trading volume, leveraging its scale to deliver deeper liquidity, sharper pricing and market insights.

item.title: A Conversation with Ken Griffin
item.dc:creator: ovaughn
item.description: Citadel Securities founder Ken Griffin spoke with Bloomberg’s Dani Burger at our recent Future of Global Markets Conference. Ken and Dani discussed the transformative potential of artificial intelligence, and how investors are becoming more discerning in this rapidly growing mark...
item.content:encoded:
Citadel Securities founder Ken Griffin spoke with Bloomberg’s Dani Burger at our recent Future of Global Markets Conference. Ken and Dani discussed the transformative potential of artificial intelligence, and how investors are becoming more discerning in this rapidly growing market. Read the key takeaways below.

1. Artificial Intelligence: Transformative Potential and the Future of Work

  • The advancement in AI models over just the past year has been absolutely tremendous. In a number of fields, AI is literally game-changing. Work that used to take our PhDs and master’s-level employees four to six weeks can now be completed in a matter of hours.
  • There are three implications:

    –  For workers: AI poses a real threat to certain white-collar jobs. We need to embrace reskilling in a profound way. There’s plenty of talk about it, but very little action.

    –  For corporate America: Competitive moats are being filled in by bulldozers. Companies will need to innovate faster, create more customer value and take costs out faster. That’s ultimately a win for the American consumer.

    –  For entrepreneurs: This is a golden era for new business formation. Startups will unleash products we’ve never even thought of and create opportunities for people who don’t have perfect pedigrees to build successful careers.

  • The history of our free market is that we go through transitions like this. They’re challenging for incumbents and difficult for workers, but ultimately our lives are better.

2. AI Markets: Investors Are Becoming More Discerning

  • For the last several years, investors have largely bought into the AI theme: We’re going to spend hundreds of billions or trillions on data centers and compute. Buy the hyperscalers, buy the chip companies, buy the entire supply chain.
  • Now we’re reaching a point where people are becoming more discerning. Who actually earns the economic rents? Where are the real supply constraints? How long will today’s extraordinary margins persist?
  • GPU overcapacity is a significant risk. GPUs have very low marginal operating costs, much like airlines. When capacity exceeds demand, pricing can go into freefall. We saw a similar dynamic during the telecom buildout in 2000, when excess fiber capacity drove telecommunications prices sharply lower.
  • Investors are also reconsidering the useful life of GPUs. Five- or six-year-old chips may command extraordinary pricing today, but that doesn’t mean those economics will persist for another five or six years. Revenue and valuation assumptions for years seven, eight and nine need to be reconsidered.
  • Corporate America is becoming much more sophisticated about extracting value from AI. Companies are asking where they truly need expensive, state-of-the-art models from OpenAI and Anthropic, and where open-source models can do the job at a fraction of the cost.
  • There is a tension between the enormous spending ambitions of foundational model companies and their customers’ efforts to maximize returns and control costs. The question is whether these models become so indispensable—potentially by solving problems like curing cancer—that customers will pay almost any price.

3. Is AI a Bubble?

  • There are almost certainly bubbles within this moment in time. Radical transformations of our economy are generally intertwined with bubbles.
  • Think about the internet in 1999 and 2000. Some companies had pretty fanciful business models, but the internet fundamentally transformed our lives. I just wish I’d kept my Amazon stock.
  • We’ve seen this with other transformative technologies, including the railroads. What’s left in the wake of these bubbles is often game-changing for the world, and the companies that emerge on the other side can be market leaders for decades.

item.title: Fireside Conversation with Eric Glyman, CEO of Ramp
item.dc:creator: ovaughn
item.description: Eric Glyman, Co-founder and CEO of Ramp, joined Frank Flight, Head of Macro Strategy at Citadel Securities, for a discussion on how AI is reshaping business operations, productivity and economic growth. Drawing on Ramp’s corporate spending data, Glyman explored the pace of AI ado...
item.content:encoded:
Eric Glyman, Co-founder and CEO of Ramp, joined Frank Flight, Head of Macro Strategy at Citadel Securities, for a discussion on how AI is reshaping business operations, productivity and economic growth. Drawing on Ramp’s corporate spending data, Glyman explored the pace of AI adoption, its implications for the workforce and the evolving economics of artificial intelligence.

Key Takeaways

  • Uneven AI Adoption: While a majority of Ramp’s customers now spend on AI, adoption remains highly concentrated, with the top 1% of businesses accounting for approximately 80% of AI spending.
  • Evolving AI Economics: Declining model costs and intensifying competition are reshaping the AI landscape, potentially shifting value toward application-layer companies that translate intelligence into business outcomes.
  • AI and Business Growth: Ramp’s research found that businesses with higher AI adoption experienced stronger revenue growth, with high-intensity adopters increasing headcount approximately 12% faster than before adoption.
  • Organizational Transformation: AI is prompting companies to rethink traditional workflows and organizational structures, integrating intelligent systems into core functions rather than simply automating individual tasks.
  • Managing AI Investment: As spending on AI becomes a significant corporate expense, businesses will increasingly need tools to manage costs, evaluate returns and optimize their use of AI.

item.content:encoded:
Jeff Maurone, Technology COO at Citadel Securities, shared how the firm leverages AI, quantitative research and proprietary technology to deliver actionable market insights and high-quality execution for clients. He highlighted the firm’s technology infrastructure, data-driven analytics and growing collaboration with clients to anticipate market dynamics and solve complex trading challenges.

Key Takeaways

  • AI-Driven Insights: AI and autonomous agents are amplifying human intuition, enabling Citadel Securities to systematically analyze vast amounts of data and answer client questions before they are asked.
  • Predictive Market Analytics: Proprietary tools such as Breakout Probability and Positioning NowCast combine market flows, positioning data and historical trends to provide earlier visibility into shifts in investor holdings.
  • Real-Time Credit Intelligence: The firm’s investment-grade credit heat map provides a customized, real-time view of corporate bond spreads, helping clients track market movements across issuers and sectors.
  • Technology at Scale: Citadel Securities’ research infrastructure supports more than 500 quantitative researchers and over 200 petabytes of data, with 65% of colleagues writing code to develop proprietary trading technology.
  • Client Collaboration: The firm has engaged with more than 100 client technology teams to explore AI adoption, agent development and quantitative research, strengthening partnerships and developing solutions to address client needs.

item.title: A Narrow Margin of Safety
item.dc:creator: ovaughn
item.description: THE SHARP SELL-OFF IN EQUITIES SUGGESTS INVESTORS ARE BECOMING MORE DEMANDING ABOUT THE RETURNS UNDERPINNING THE AI BUILDOUT…and less willing to assume that extraordinary spending will translate into equally extraordinary profits. In my mind, higher yields have made those questio...
item.content:encoded:
THE SHARP SELL-OFF IN EQUITIES SUGGESTS INVESTORS ARE BECOMING MORE DEMANDING ABOUT THE RETURNS UNDERPINNING THE AI BUILDOUT…and less willing to assume that extraordinary spending will translate into equally extraordinary profits. In my mind, higher yields have made those questions more urgent, whilst the scale of investment commitments has made the answers more consequential. The scrutiny spans the entire chain…whether customers generate sufficient productivity gains, whether model developers retain enough pricing power and whether infrastructure revenues adequately compensate for financing costs and depreciation. Capex itself has become a two-sided risk: spending cuts raise questions about the durability of the investment cycle…whilst further increases raise questions about financing, execution, and the eventual returns. Meta’s latest results illustrate the scale of the commitment: Q3 revenues grew 26% YoY, yet $34.9bn of capex (including finance-lease principal payments) exceeded $32.8bn of operating cash flow…leaving quarterly free cash flow at -$2.1bn. Its full-year guidance implies another ~$49–59bn of spending in Q4. The eventual returns may justify that expenditure…but investors need greater confidence that the capacity can be financed, delivered, and monetised on the promised timetable. I remain of the view that demand for intelligence is strong, but the economics require more discrimination. Ramp’s data are instructive…token spending was virtually flat through August and September even as volumes increased, with falling prices and improving efficiency explaining much of the divergence. Spending subsequently reached a new high in early October, albeit with slower growth. These observations come from Ramp’s customer base rather than the entire economy…but they caution against interpreting weaker dollar-spending growth as an equivalent slowdown in usage. DeepSeek’s DeepInfer release illustrates how software improvements can increase the useful output from existing hardware…adding uncertainty around how much incremental capacity will be required to serve future AI demand, even as cheaper inference encourages greater usage. Cheaper intelligence improves customer economics and expands the range of viable applications. For suppliers, profitability depends on how quickly costs fall relative to prices, how much additional usage follows, and the investment required to serve it. A successful technology can create enormous economic value whilst leaving some of its producers earning disappointing returns. This continues to favour diversified platforms with established cash flows and several routes to monetisation…although even their shareholders need to distinguish between funding the next stage of growth and earning an attractive return from it.

 

 

THE INDUSTRY IS CONFRONTING THESE ECONOMIC QUESTIONS WITH LIMITED POLITICAL GOODWILL. A Reuters/Ipsos poll this month found that 69% of Democratic registered voters supported limits on datacentre construction, alongside 43% of Republicans…a reminder that opposition extends across party lines. The November midterms could bring greater congressional scrutiny, whilst state and local elections matter directly for permitting and the conditions attached to development. A sweeping federal restriction or even just additional compliance requirements, local construction limits and prolonged approvals could all make deployment slower and more expensive. For leveraged projects, delays can mean additional interest expense before revenues arrive and potentially a different competitive landscape by the time the capacity becomes operational. It’s important to remember that scarcity today provides limited assurance about the returns on capacity delivered several years from now. Projects could be delayed by power constraints and permitting, only to arrive into a market where efficiency has improved, competing supply has increased and pricing is less favourable than originally assumed. The cyber news this week also adds to the political risk. AI-assisted researchers helped uncover critical vulnerabilities in the widely used PHP software that had existed for more than a decade, whilst Amazon has identified exploitation attempts and warned that AI is shortening the time required to turn vulnerability information into working attacks. The technology is improving our ability to identify weaknesses whilst also making them easier to exploit. These are serious engineering and security problems requiring stronger controls, faster patching, and continued investment in defensive capabilities. My concern is that legitimate security concerns become a justification for broad restrictions that impede productive deployment. The economic costs of the political response could extend well beyond the vulnerabilities being addressed – another risk to the timing of returns when so much prospective growth depends on the pace of AI adoption.

 

 

THESE DEVELOPMENTS ARE ARRIVING AFTER A SUCCESSION OF POLICY CHOICES THAT HAVE MADE THE ECONOMY MORE EXPENSIVE TO FINANCE AND OPERATE. Procyclical fiscal easing has supported demand and increased borrowing requirements, whilst tariffs have added costs and uncertainty…compounding the challenge of bringing inflation sustainably back to target. Stronger growth and productive investment also explain part of the increase in real yields; some of the higher cost of capital reflects better opportunities to deploy it. Nevertheless, the cumulative burden matters…higher rates progressively reach borrowers as debt refinances, higher input costs squeeze margins or reach consumers, and persistent inflation makes monetary accommodation more difficult. An economy can absorb these pressures whilst investment, earnings and confidence remain strong…but resilience should not be confused with the costs disappearing. Moreover, the energy shock continues with Brent trading above $117/bbl. this week as attacks in Saudi Arabia and around Gulf shipping renewed concerns about disruption, despite resilient regional crude exports. Sustained energy costs absorb purchasing power and raise operating expenses. An AI-led investment slowdown alongside renewed energy disruption would leave the Fed confronting weaker prospective growth and an uncomfortable inflation backdrop. It also seems that the midterms will not clear the geopolitical risk with reports of preparations for possible renewed strikes against Iran after the election. Divided government would also create uncertainty about Washington’s capacity to respond to the fiscal trajectory. These risks are now beginning to reinforce one another. An equity correction can be absorbed…but a sustained retrenchment in investment and financing would threaten the growth, earnings and household wealth that have helped the US economy withstand higher costs. Even lower Treasury yields would provide limited relief to borrowers whose credit spreads widen sufficiently to offset them…risk-free yields can fall whilst the cost of financing risk rises. In sum, these concerns have been accumulating for some time, but the strength of the growth and AI narrative has allowed markets to look past them…but as confidence in that narrative weakens, those pressures become harder to absorb. With so much of the economy and stock market now levered to the AI trade, there is precious little margin for error just as the other risks threaten to bite.
